engine_name: Lifeline Daily Protein Target engine v2 (DEC-86): referral stops (kidney, liver or recovery, clinician plan), WHO pregnancy and breastfeeding branch, one sourced winning band for healthy adults, 2.0 g/kg ceiling, continuous basis weight
intended_use: Educational screening aid that estimates a daily protein intake target (grams per day, g/kg and per meal) for healthy adults from published guidelines and trials. It is not a prescription, not a diagnosis and not individualised clinical nutrition advice.
eligibility: Adults aged 18 to 99. No number is given, and the visitor is referred to their clinician, for kidney disease or dialysis, liver disease or recovery from a serious illness, injury or surgery, or a diet or protein plan from a doctor or dietitian. Pregnancy and breastfeeding use their own WHO branch. Kidney function "not sure" gives a number with a caution. Not for children.
sources: WHO/FAO/UNU (2007). Protein and amino acid requirements in human nutrition. WHO Technical Report Series 935. Safe level 0.83 g/kg; pregnancy +1, +9, +31 g a day by trimester; breastfeeding +19 g (first 6 months), +12.5 g after.
Institute of Medicine (2005). Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids. RDA 0.8 g/kg.
Bhasin S et al. (2018). Effect of protein intake on lean body mass in functionally limited older men (OPTIMen). JAMA Intern Med 178:530-541.
Tagawa R et al. (2021). Dose-response relationship between protein intake and muscle mass increase. Nutr Rev 79:66-75.

Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM (2016). Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and the American College of Sports Medicine: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. 1.2-2.0 g/kg.
Jäger R et al. (2017). ISSN Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr 14:20. 1.4-2.0 g/kg; 20-40 g per meal.
Morton RW et al. (2018). Protein supplementation and resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength. Br J Sports Med 52:376-384.
Leidy HJ et al. (2015). The role of protein in weight loss and maintenance. Am J Clin Nutr 101:1320S-1329S. 1.2-1.6 g/kg.
Wycherley TP et al. (2012). Energy-restricted high-protein vs standard-protein diets: meta-analysis. Am J Clin Nutr 96:1281-1298.
Bauer J et al. (2013). PROT-AGE Study Group recommendations. J Am Med Dir Assoc 14:542-559. 1.0-1.2 g/kg.
Deutz NEP et al. (2014). ESPEN Expert Group: protein intake and exercise with aging. Clin Nutr 33:929-936. 1.2-1.5 g/kg when active or ill.
Volkert D et al. (2019). ESPEN guideline on clinical nutrition and hydration in geriatrics. Clin Nutr. At least 1.0 g/kg.
Nunes EA et al. (2022). Protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults. J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 13:795-810.
KDIGO (2024). Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of CKD; KDOQI (2020) nutrition in CKD. Basis for the kidney referral.
Plauth M et al. (2019). ESPEN guideline on clinical nutrition in liver disease. Basis for the liver referral.
NICE NG246 (2025). Overweight and obesity management: lower BMI cut-offs for the healthy range shown.
limitations: Population guideline and trial figures, not individual requirements; the tool cannot see kidney function tests, protein quality, energy balance, medications or conditions beyond the questions asked.
The 2.0 g/kg ceiling is the scope of this general tool, not a safety limit.
Basis weight above the BMI 24.9 weight counts 40 % of the extra weight; this is a dietetic convention, not a guideline figure.
Underweight (BMI < 18.5) visitors get the standard computation with a supportive message; no energy or weight-gain advice is given.
ORC-02 v2 was written from DEC-86 alone and agrees on every fixture; it detects implementation errors, not errors in the approved rules.
regulatory_statement: Confirmed by the clinical reviewer at HG-02 (27 Oct 2026, Part D). The tool gives general wellbeing information from published guidelines and trials; it does not diagnose, treat or recommend treatment, gives no number where a clinician must set the amount, and every result carries the not-a-diagnosis statement. It is operated as an educational and screening information service and is not placed on the market as a medical device.
licence: Site content © Lifeline Daily. Guideline figures are facts from the cited publications; no third-party code is embedded in the engine.
